t.1.74.1: Śukra said: Know this, Devayānī: the man who always bears patiently the insults of others has conquered this whole world.
t.1.74.2: He who restrains his risen anger as one restrains a horse is called a true charioteer by the good, not he who merely hangs on to the reins.
t.1.74.3: He who drives out anger that has arisen by means of non-anger, know this, Devayānī, by him this whole world is conquered.
t.1.74.4: He who here casts off anger that has arisen by means of forbearance, as a snake casts off its worn-out skin, is truly called a man.
t.1.74.5: He who restrains his anger, who patiently endures harsh words, and who, though tormented, does not torment others, is surely a worthy vessel of prosperity.
t.1.74.6: One who sacrifices tirelessly month after month for a hundred years, and one who never grows angry at anyone: of the two, the one free from anger is the greater.
t.1.74.7: Whatever enmity thoughtless boys and girls may engage in, a wise man should not imitate it, for they do not know what is strong and what is weak.
t.1.74.8: Father, though I am only a girl, I know what difference there is here between the dharmas of forbearance and of insulting speech, and I know too their strength and weakness.
t.1.74.9: One who wishes to prosper should not forgive a pupil who does not behave as a pupil should. Therefore I have no wish to live among those whose conduct is so corrupt.
t.1.74.11: But among those good people who recognize a man by his conduct and his lineage, one should dwell; that dwelling is said to be the best.
t.1.74.10: Those men who revile a person for his conduct and his lineage, a wise man who seeks his own welfare should not dwell among such evil-minded people.
t.1.74.12: The words of Vṛṣaparvan's daughter were an evil utterance, most dreadful. For I think there is nothing harder than this even in the three worlds: that one bereft of fortune should wait upon the blazing fortune of a rival.
